title: Elastic weight onramp and failure mitigation
body:
Purpose and high level idea:

This note sketches an "elastic onramp" for weights — a runtime component that brings model parameters online progressively and safely, while providing deterministic fallbacks and graceful degradation when IO or memory constraints occur. The onramp sits between the storage layer (safely-encoded safetensors or mmapped shards) and the serving scheduler/kernel layer.

Goals:
- Allow per-layer / per-shard demand-driven activation so cold-starts are bounded by useful-first latency rather than full-model IO.
- Provide safety checks and automatic mitigation when weight load fails (corrupt shards, partial network loss, OOM).
- Integrate with KV cache warming and kernel selection so we avoid catastrophic slow-path execution.
- Enable hot-swap of repaired/updated shards without global inference interruption.

Design primitives and responsibilities:

1) Onramp: a stateful weight activation controller
- Tracks per-model, per-shard state: UNKNOWN -> PENDING -> RESIDENT -> DEGRADED -> EVICTED. States are strings here, stored in the local node metadata store.
- Exposes a simple api to scheduler: request_activation(layer_id, priority_hint, request_id) -> activation_handle.
- Activation is idempotent: multiple callers for same layer join the same activation future.

2) Progressive load strategy:
- Head-first: layers required for initial token generations (embedding, first transformer blocks, positional embeddings) are prioritized for synchronous activation.
- Lazy tail: large dense layers and attention value matrices are loaded lazily when execution reaches them.
- Streamed safetensors: when source supports ranged reads, fetch chunks for a single weight tensor progressively and verify checksums per-chunk. This allows starting with a lower precision/quantized prefix and patching later.

3) Memory accounting and temporary staging:
- Two-stage residency: stage buffers (pinned CUDA staging) for incoming tensors, then atomic attach into the resident map.
- If staging buffer allocation fails, fall back to: a) quantized variant (if available) b) CPU-mapped view (mmap) with smaller working set c) block execution until critical layers available (last resort).
- A resident byte accounting ledger communicates with the eviction controller so onramp can request soft evictions with priorities.

4) Integrity and rollback:
- Per-shard checksum (sha256) stored in metadata. Onramp validates after full chunked transfer and before commit.
- If checksum mismatch, mark shard as CORRUPT and attempt N fallback sources (local cache, remote store, artifact-proxy). If all fail, mark layer as DEGRADED.
- DEGRADED layer: runtime switches to an alternative execution plan (smaller attention head count, quantized kernel, or CPU fallback) when possible. Log and attach trace id to request.

5) Hot-swap protocol for patched shards:
- Patch path: a new shard version arrives (hot-redeploy). Onramp downloads into staging area, validates, then swaps pointers atomically with old shard.
- During swap, any in-flight inference referencing old tensors continues using a read-only view until the reference count hits zero; new requests get the updated shard.
- If swap commit fails, rollback to old pointer and mark new version as FAILED.

6) Scheduler interaction and backpressure:
- Activation calls return either: READY, IN_PROGRESS, or QUEUED. The scheduler uses this to decide whether to route a request to an alternative model variant, enqueue, or serve degraded output.
- Backpressure tokens: the onramp issues limited concurrent load permits. If permits exhausted, callers receive FAST_FAIL or DEGRADED response depending on policy.
- Integrate with the kernel scheduler: when a layer is requested with high priority, kernel executor can preempt low-priority batches to make room for critical activation tasks.

7) KV cache co-warming:
- When a new request triggers activation of layers important for KV operations (key/projector + attention kernels), the onramp signals the KV cache manager to prefetch recent keys for that model instance from remote cache (if local miss).
- If layer is DEGRADED, we avoid warming KV for that request to reduce wasted IO.

Failure modes and mitigations (practical examples):

Scenario A: Network partition during chunked safetensors stream\- The onramp should keep partial chunks in staging with timestamps. After a short retry window (configurable, default 5s), switch to nearest mirror or remote artifact-cache. Requests depending on the missing layer should be routed to a quantized variant or to a cheaper model.

Scenario B: GPU OOM during atomic attach\- The atomic attach fails because there is insufficient free GPU memory. Mitigation order:
1) Try to ask eviction controller for N bytes (soft eviction of LRU shards).
2) If eviction yields insufficient memory and request is high-priority, pause lower priority execution to drain KV cache entries or transient activations.
3) If still insufficient, attach on CPU-mmap and allow kernel to run slower path.
4) Emit metric runtime.onramp.attach.failure and trace with memory snapshot.

Scenario C: Corrupt shard checksum\- Attempt failover sources in this order: local object cache -> regional artifact proxy -> origin store. If all fail, mark layer DEGRADED and route requests to fallback model. Send an automated incident note tagged "artifact-corruption".

Operational considerations and instrumentation:
- Metrics to emit: activation.latency (by layer), activation.failures.by-cause, activation.state_transitions, staging.buffer_wait_time, swap.commit.latency, percent_degraded_serves, kv-warm-success-rate.
- Tracing: include activation id in request traces and keep span for activation stages (enqueue, fetch, verify, attach, commit).
- Alerts: sustained activation.latency > 2x baseline AND percent_degraded_serves > 5% for 10m -> P1.

Testing strategy and canary rollout:
- Unit tests: simulate chunked reads and intentional checksum failures.
- Integration: loopback environment where we can crash the artifact proxy mid-stream and verify graceful fallback.
- Canary: ramp for new onramp in three phases: internal QA -> small percent of traffic with read-only metrics -> canary replace in a single region for non-critical customers -> global rollout.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Granularity: should onramp operate at per-tensor, per-layer, or per-shard granularity? Recommendation: per-shard for IO efficiency but expose per-tensor hooks for kernels that can accept partial weight availability.
- Quantized-fallback library: finalize API and format expectations (native int8 tensors vs compressed blocks).
- Swap atomicity: how to implement lightweight RCU-style pointer swaps for CUDA memory handles across multiple processes in the same node? Investigate cross-process shared handle patterns on Linux + NVML.
- Eviction policy integration: define clear SLA mapping from model tier -> eviction priority.

Appendix: quick pseudocode for activation flow:

function request_activation(layer_id, priority):
  if state(layer_id) == RESIDENT: return READY
  if existing_future(layer_id): join and wait with timeout -> return state or IN_PROGRESS
  mark state PENDING, enqueue fetch task with priority
  return IN_PROGRESS

fetch task:
  open source stream (range-capable ideally)
  loop read chunk -> verify chunk checksum -> append staging buffer
  on full tensor, compute full checksum -> if ok then attempt atomic attach into resident map (with memory reservation check) -> if attach ok set RESIDENT else attempt mitigations -> set state appropriately

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a pragmatic mix of engineering and operational controls rather than a formal RFC. The goal is to capture realistic tradeoffs we encountered in last quarter's incidents and propose a compact component that teams can iterate on.
- If we agree on the core states and failure semantics, I will follow up with a sequence diagram and a minimal API proto for the activation handle.

Known related docs: weight-residency-controller-and-async-load-playbook.json (existing), resumable-weight-snapshots-and-kv-consistency-playbook.json (existing). This doc tries to sit orthogonal by prioritizing progressive onramp, hot-swap safety, and tight scheduler interaction rather than focusing purely on low-level mmap implementation details.

Immediate next steps:
- Review with storage and kernels team (ask: Aaron for safetensors chunk spec, Priya for kernel fallback hooks).
- Prototype a small server that implements chunked safetensors streaming + staged attach and run it against synthetic 70B model shards.
- Add smoke tests that exercise hot-swap during heavy QPS.

Unresolved action items (owners):
- Aaron: sample artifact proxy mirror behavior and HTTP range support (due 2025-03-11).
- Priya: propose kernel-level fallback API surface (due 2025-03-18).
- Marcus: prototype onramp thread pool and staging buffer lifecycle (due 2025-04-01).
